newsitem.title: LEBANON: Hariri snubs parliament but wins confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Hariri snubs parliament but wins confidence vote.

text.p: Lebanon's Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri stormed out of parliament on Thursday in a clash over soaring government borrowing but then easily survived a vote of confidence taken after he left.
Hariri walked out angrily after the house approved a non-binding resolution intended to commit his government to seek authorisation for each loan it wants to raise.

"We want you to pledge that there will be no treasury borrowing without going back to parliament in compliance with the law and constitution," parliament Speaker Nabih Berri told Hariri before the vote on the resolution.
After Hariri left, the house rejected by 69 votes to seven a separate motion of no confidence in his performance as minister of posts and communications, one of two additional portfolios he holds.
The resolution on borrowing, proposed by former prime minister Selim al-Hoss, said: "The government pledges to comply with the law and constitution in treasury borrowing matters".
Deputies said it was a rap on the knuckles for the government, which has accumulated a growing mountain of debt reaching 83 percent of GDP, but did not oblige it to comply.
"This resolution clearly condemns the government," former speaker Hussein Husseini told Reuters. "But it is a dialogue of the deaf between the government and parliament."

Opposition deputy Nasib Lahoud said it was not clear whether the government would now seek approval for further borrowing. "I cannot predict their behaviour but I think they must think about this," said.
Deputies said the resolution was an attempt to force the government to honour its constitutional obligation to obtain parliamentary approval for all borrowing.

Parliament was concerned that while the 1997 budget law it approved in January authorised government borrowing to cover a planned 36 percent annual deficit of income against expenditure, the deficit had ballooned to 60 percent at the end of April.
A deputy said the house believed the government was borrowing over the 36 percent ceiling without seeking its approval.

Lebanon's total domestic and foreign debt rose in the first four months of the year by nearly $1 billion to $11.6 billion. This compares with an estimated GDP (Gross Domestic Product) of $13.9 billion at the end of 1996.
